newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - JGBs to strive to emerge from shadows.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - JGBs to strive to emerge from shadows.

text.p: Japanese government bonds (JGBs) may be preparing to come out from under the pall cast by the volatile equity and currency markets, analysts said on Monday.

Some analysts said there are signs the yen is stabilising, and coupled with JGBs' earlier rally to record highs, domestic investors could be wooed back again. But overseas investors are still likely to be wary.

"For Japanese pension funds, for example, it is very tempting at the moment to take profits in U.S. Treasuries and head for shelter from a rate rise in JGBs," said Kirit Shah, chief market strategist at Sanwa International in London.
"But for overseas people, you would have to be quite bullish on yen to be interested," he said.
He said even if the U.S. Federal Reserve does not raise U.S. interest rates imminently, there were few signs that Treasuries had any further to go.
Also, there will be a temptation for Japanese investors to repatriate their capital ahead of the fiscal year-end in March, which could mean U.S. bonds suffer from the capital outflow.
Such capital is unlikely to be placed in the Japanese equity market, particularly after Monday's performace.
The Nikkei fell two percent as investors sold bank shares after rumours that a major Japanese bank would make large derivatives losses. It shed more than 354 points to end the session at 17,334.90.
At the same time, the March bond future hit a record high of 126.83, although it later gave up some of its gains. The benchmark 182nd JGB is currently yielding 2.35 percent.
Peter Wilson, yen strategist at Tokyo Mitsubishi in London, said however it was not a forgone conclusion that a Nikkei level of 16,000-17,000 would automatically be good for bonds.
"The lower the Nikkei goes, the less there's an obvious negative correlation," said Wilson. "If the Nikkei fails to recover by the end of February, we could see profit taking in bonds."
He said he would like to see the rise in futures more supported by cash buying than has recently been the case.

Alan Capper, bond strategist at Paribas Capital Markets in London, said Tuesday's auction of 10-year bonds was crucial, since the rally may not be sustainable. The last auction of 10-year JGBs carried a record low 2.7 percent coupon.
"Everything depends on the auction," said Capper. "I'd be a buyer if the bid-to-cover ratio was four and a half."
Shah said there could be another push to reach 2.25 percent on the 182nd bond.

Analysts said worries that the forthcoming hike in consumption tax would depress economic growth had been overdone, but were difficult to quantify. On April 1, consumption tax will rise to five percent from the current three percent.

"When you look at fiscal contractions, they usually don't have more than a quarter-on-quarter effect," said Wilson. "We're relatively upbeat. While consumption tax will take cash out of people's pockets, cuts in car tax and the cost of long-distance phone calls are putting cash back."

Shah advised buying 15- to 20-year JGBs and selling the 10-year area on a duration adjusted basis to obtain neutrality to a yield curve shift. He said the spread between the 10s and 20s would narrow to 50 basis points from its current level of about 70 basis points.
Yamaichi suggested selling the 164th 2003 bond and buying the 188th 2006 for a pick up of about 45 basis points.
"The gloom about financial markets is making people ignore the economy," said Shah. "Okay, it isn't bullish, but it is rising. Don't get too negative on the real economy."
